opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd frame it less as "a better chance" and more as timing and fit. When we started thinking about building a company around inference infrastructure, the question for everyone on the original vLLM team was what stage of life and career they were in.

Zhuohan had already made his own choices about where he wanted to go next, and I really respect that. He's one of the people who shaped vLLM from day one, and someone like that has many good options. I didn't want to push him into something that wasn't his own conviction.

With WooSuk, the conversations felt more natural. We'd spent a lot of time together on the engineering side, on the scheduler, the model runner, all the unglamorous parts that make the system actually work. We had a shared sense of what was still unfinished and what the project needed to look like in a few years. When you both feel there's still a big unsolved problem in front of you, and you both want to be the ones to solve it, recruiting is almost just saying that out loud.

So I wouldn't call it a calculation about who was easier to get. It was more about who, at that moment, wanted the same thing I wanted. In open-source teams especially, you can't really convince someone to join. You can only find out whether you're already aligned.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't that I thought one of them was better than the other. They're both exceptional. It was more about where each of them was in their life and what they wanted.

Zhuohan, by the time I got to know him well, had basically already made up his mind. He wanted to go to a frontier lab and work on the model side. He was very clear about it. When someone has that kind of clarity, you can tell that whatever you offer, you're competing against something they've already decided on. And OpenAI is not an easy thing to compete with for a young researcher. So I never seriously thought I could pull him over.

WooSuk was different. WooSuk is the kind of person who is really attached to the system itself. vLLM is in a sense his child. He wrote the first PagedAttention kernel, he cared about every performance regression, he would reply to issues at two in the morning. For him, the question was never "which company," it was "where can this project live and grow." That's a question I actually had an answer to. If you can show someone like that a place where the project stays open, stays central, and he still gets to make the technical decisions, then you have a real conversation.

There's also a practical thing. I had been working with WooSuk day to day for a long time in the vLLM community, reviewing each other's code, arguing about design. So there was trust already. With Zhuohan, we were colleagues on the project, but the day-to-day overlap was smaller. Recruiting is really about trust more than about the offer, and I simply had more of it with WooSuk.

So it wasn't that I rated them differently. It was that one of them was looking for exactly what I could give, and the other was looking for something I couldn't.

r001.rationale: The response says Zhuohan had decided to join a frontier lab, but does not identify disruption to his existing team as a recruiting obstacle.

r002.rationale: The response attributes WooSuk’s recruitability to his connection to vLLM, alignment with the project’s needs, and existing trust; it does not say he was not yet deeply involved in his existing company.
